questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Acute Angle Between a Vector and a Subspace Spanned by Orthogonal Vectors
questions.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the subspace $S=\text{Span}{v,w},$ where

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the acute angle between $x$ and the subspace $S$ given that the set ${v,w}$ is orthogonal.
questions.worked_solution:
Since the set ${v,w}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{v}x+{\text{proj}}_{w}x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}{v}$ and $\text{Span}{w}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{v}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot v}{v\cdot v}v=\frac{3\cdot 1+3\cdot 1+0\cdot 1}{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}v=2[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{w}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot w}{w\cdot w}w=\frac{3\cdot 2+3\cdot (-1)+0\cdot (-1)}{{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}w=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The acute angle between $x$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $x$ and ${\text{proj}}_{S}x$ or any other non-zero vector that is parallel to ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ So, to make calculations easier, we can find the angle between the vectors

$\,$ $x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{2}{3}{\text{proj}}_{S}x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{3\cdot 2+3\cdot 1+0\cdot 1}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{3}^{2}+{0}^{2}}\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{9}{\sqrt{18}\sqrt{6}} \\  & =\frac{9}{6\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})=\frac{\pi }{6},
$$

which is already an acute angle.

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Distance Between a Vector and a Subspace Spanned by Orthogonal Vectors
questions.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the subspace $S=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ -4\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the distance between $x$ and the subspace $S$ given that the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is orthogonal.
questions.worked_solution:
Since the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}{{a}_{1}}$ and $\text{Span}{{a}_{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}=\frac{2\cdot 1+2\cdot 1+(-4)\cdot 4}{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{4}^{2}}{a}_{1}=(-\frac{2}{3})[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{2\cdot 2+2\cdot 2+(-4)\cdot (-1)}{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{4}{3}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x \\  & =(-\frac{2}{3})[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]+\frac{4}{3}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{2}{3}([\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1 \\ -4\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 4 \\ -2\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ -4\end{aligned}]=x.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $x$ coincides with the projection, the distance between $x$ and the subspace $S$ is zero $0.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto a Plane
questions.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the plane $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 3 \\ -3\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}-18 \\ -16 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the plane given that $v⊥w.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}{v,w}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ 
And, since the set ${v,w}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by 

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}{{a}_{1}}$ and $\text{Span}{{a}_{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{v}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot v}{v\cdot v}v=\frac{(-18)\cdot (-2)+(-16)\cdot 2+1\cdot 4}{(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}+{4}^{2}}v=\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{w}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot w}{w\cdot w}w=\frac{(-18)\cdot (-3)+(-16)\cdot 3+1\cdot (-3)}{(-3)^{2}+{3}^{2}+(-3)^{2}}w=\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 3 \\ -3\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}([\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Distance Between a Vector and a Subspace Spanned by Orthogonal Vectors
questions.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the subspace $S=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3 \\ -5 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the distance between $x$ and the subspace $S$ given that the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is orthogonal.
questions.worked_solution:
Since the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}{{a}_{1}}$ and $\text{Span}{{a}_{2}}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}=\frac{2\cdot 0+3\cdot 1+(-5)\cdot (-1)+2\cdot 2}{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{(-1)}^{2}+{2}^{2}}{a}_{1}=2[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ -2 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{2\cdot 3+3\cdot 1+(-5)\cdot (-1)+2\cdot (-1)}{{3}^{2}+{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ -2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3 \\ -3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]=\overset{^}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the distance between $x$ and the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}d(x,\overset{^}{x}) & =‖x-\overset{^}{x}‖ \\  & =\sqrt{({x}_{1}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{1})^{2}+({x}_{2}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{2})^{2}+({x}_{3}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{3})^{2}+({x}_{4}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{4})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(2-3)^{2}+(3-3)^{2}+(-5-(-3))^{2}+(2-3)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Acute Angle Between a Vector and a Subspace Spanned by Orthogonal Vectors
questions.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the subspace $S=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

 
Find the acute angle between $x$ and the subspace $S$ given that the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is orthogonal. Round the answer to $2$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
Since the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}{{a}_{1}}$ and $\text{Span}{{a}_{2}}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}=\frac{4\cdot 1+0\cdot 0+2\cdot (-1)}{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{(-1)}^{2}}{a}_{1}=\frac{2}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{4\cdot 1+0\cdot 1+2\cdot 1}{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{2}=2[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The acute angle between $x$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $x$ and ${\text{proj}}_{S}x$ or any other non-zero vector that is parallel to ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ 

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{x\cdot {\text{proj}}_{S}\,x}{‖x‖\,‖{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x‖} \\  & =\frac{4\cdot 3+0\cdot 2+2\cdot 1}{\sqrt{{4}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}}\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{14}{\sqrt{20}\sqrt{14}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{14}}{\sqrt{20}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{7}{10}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\sqrt{\frac{7}{10}})≈{33.21}^{∘},
$$

which is already an acute angle.
